feed.title: Wits AHEAD · Daily briefing
feed.subtitle: News, research, video and readings on AI, data and human capability in higher education, curated every morning.
feed.rights: Wits AHEAD Research Group, Wits School of Education, University of the Witwatersrand

entry.title: New framework argues the cost of AI essay-marking systems should be measured against trustworthy scores, not efficiency alone
entry.summary:
A new paper proposes a “Cost-Aware Measurement Design” framework for automated essay-scoring systems, arguing that the computing cost of AI marking is usually treated as a technical efficiency question when it is really a measurement-design choice. The framework defines a “cost per defensible score” that compares scoring systems only among designs meeting a minimum standard of trustworthy measurement, and treats an institution's governance and oversight capacity as a limit on which designs can be used at all, rather than as a price to be minimised away.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, the framework gives universities considering AI-assisted marking a concrete way to ask whether a cheaper system is actually producing defensible scores, rather than judging automated assessment tools on speed and cost alone.

arXiv (preprint) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: Study of a South African university finds online “participation profiles” mostly track how long a learner is observed, not how engaged they are
entry.summary:
Analysing 16,448 learner-course records from 4,599 students across 152 courses at a South African public university, researchers tested eight commonly used measures of online “participation” and found that all of them tracked how long a learner was observed in a course more closely than how actively the learner took part. After adjusting for this, a smaller set of measures still grouped learners into a broad two-profile pattern and a more detailed four-profile pattern, but only with moderate confidence.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and predictive analytics for student success, the finding is a direct caution for early-warning and retention systems built on South African data: unless the length of time a learner is tracked is accounted for, a learner flagged as “disengaged” may simply be one who was observed for less time, not one genuinely at risk.

arXiv (preprint) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: Study finds students who earn the same grade can have done very different amounts of their own thinking with AI help
entry.summary:
Analysing 150 recorded conversations between students and generative AI tools, a new study finds that students who direct the AI, integrate its output critically and evaluate it carefully can earn the same grade as students who let the AI do most of the thinking for them, so the final mark alone does not show how much of the work was genuinely the student's own. The author calls this gap “epistemic ownership” and argues that grading on output alone can reward very different levels of student engagement with the same score.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, the study strengthens the case for assessment that also looks at how a student used AI during a task, not only at the finished product, since two identical grades can hide very different learning.

arXiv (preprint) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: Wits tells top applicants AI should make graduates indispensable, not just employable
entry.summary:
More than 200 top-performing matriculants from Gauteng and further afield attended the Wits Vice-Chancellor's Top Applicants Event, where Wits alumnus Dr Craig Wing gave the keynote on artificial intelligence and the future world of work. Deputy Vice-Chancellor Professor Garth Stevens told the learners that university is a responsibility rather than only a route to employment, and that Wits wants its graduates to be more than employable: it wants them to be indispensable.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, the event shows the University itself preparing incoming students for an AI-reshaped labour market from their first encounter with Wits, rather than leaving the question of employability until after graduation.

Wits University · University announcement

entry.title: Study finds AI grading tools miss most student misconceptions despite accurate scores
entry.summary:
A new study has examined whether large language models grading open-ended assignments in higher education are as useful as their accuracy scores suggest. Analysing 3,041 student responses to 50 open-ended computer science questions, scored by both human instructors and three commercial large language models, the researchers found that AI-generated feedback identified student misconceptions in only 5 to 7 per cent of cases, compared with 15 to 31 per cent for human teachers, and that AI feedback stayed uniformly positive regardless of answer quality. The study also found that AI-generated rubric sub-scores were so closely correlated with one another that they added little independent diagnostic information.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, the finding that AI grading can look accurate while missing most of the reasoning errors that matter for teaching is a caution against treating automated marking as a substitute for a teacher's diagnostic judgement.

arXiv (preprint) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: California requires its public colleges to set AI procurement and training standards
entry.summary:
California has signed into law Assembly Bill 2392, requiring its Community Colleges and California State University systems to jointly convene a working group that will recommend procurement standards and staff and student training for generative AI systems, with recommendations due by January 2028. Chaptered on 30 September 2026 as Chapter 855 of the Statutes of 2026, the law also requires both systems to review AI training at least once a year and to report to the state legislature within 60 days of signing any systemwide generative AI contract.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, California's move to put public procurement and training standards into law, rather than leaving generative AI adoption to individual institutions, is a Global North example of system-level AI governance that Global South higher education systems are also being urged to build.

California State Legislature · State legislation

entry.title: University of Johannesburg vice-chancellor: Africa needs AI governance beyond regulation
entry.summary:
In a CNBC Africa fireside chat, University of Johannesburg Vice-Chancellor Professor Letlhokwa Mpedi discussed with the channel's editor-in-chief Godfrey Mutizwa what it will take to govern artificial intelligence across Africa beyond simply regulating it. The conversation covers the role universities and policymakers should play in shaping AI's development on the continent, rather than only responding to rules set elsewhere.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, a sitting South African vice-chancellor making the case for Africa-led AI governance speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's own mission of building African capability to set the terms of AI's development, not simply comply with frameworks designed elsewhere.

CNBC Africa · Broadcast interview, major African business channel

entry.title: Joining up AI across recruitment, retention and alumni relations can close graduation gaps, if it is governed well
entry.summary:
Writing in University World News, IREX project director Cameron Mirza argues universities should treat recruitment, retention and alumni relations as one connected, AI supported lifecycle rather than separate systems with separate data. He cites Georgia State University's chatbot and predictive analytics programme, credited with cutting "summer melt" by about 21 per cent and with helping Black, Hispanic, first generation and low income students graduate at rates matching or exceeding the wider student body, while warning that models trained on historical data can also entrench the inequities they are meant to fix.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and predictive analytics for student success, the piece is a useful reminder that early warning and retention tools only close equity gaps when they are paired with human oversight and bias testing, exactly the governance question Wits AHEAD asks of any analytics tool it recommends.

University World News · Established higher education press (commentary by a sector practitioner)

entry.title: Wits researchers argue Africa must set its own AI research agenda, not just apply others' tools
entry.summary:
Two University of the Witwatersrand computer scientists, Benjamin Rosman and Steve James, who co-direct the Robotics, Autonomous Intelligence and Learning (RAIL) Lab, argue that Africa should drive artificial intelligence research rather than only apply tools built elsewhere. They point to the Deep Learning Indaba, now the world's largest AI summer school, which drew 1,300 participants to last year's gathering in Kigali and runs its IndabaX programme in 48 of Africa's 54 countries this year, and to Wits's new Machine Intelligence and Neural Discovery (MIND) Institute, which brings together about 65 academics across computer science, neuroscience, psychology and policy.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the warning against Africa becoming merely "a site for other people to do science" speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's own mission of building African led capability to set AI research questions, not only to use AI tools designed elsewhere.

Times Higher Education · Established higher education press

entry.title: Study of students in China, Japan and Mongolia finds access to generative AI does not guarantee it is useful for learning
entry.summary:
A working paper studying 42 undergraduates at one university each in China, Japan and Mongolia finds that how students reach generative AI, directly, through global platforms, or by switching language, shapes whether it is genuinely useful to them, not simply whether they can access it. Mongolian students, for example, often switched to English when Mongolian language outputs fell short, while all three groups weighed accuracy, privacy, dependence and the tool's effect on their own critical thinking. The authors, Ming Li, Qin Xie, Ariunaa Enkhtur, Lilan Chen and Fei Cheng, conclude that technological access alone does not ensure equivalent educational use across different language and technology settings.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, the finding that language and local technology conditions, not connectivity alone, decide whether generative AI genuinely helps students learn is a caution Wits AHEAD applies equally to English dominant AI tools used across multilingual Southern African campuses.

arXiv (working paper) · Working paper (preprint, not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: South African minister tells universities to move from AI debate to decisions on teaching and research
entry.summary:
Addressing the 4th Universities South Africa Higher Education Conference on 7 October 2026, Higher Education and Training Minister Buti Manamela told universities that artificial intelligence makes their core role of teaching critical thinking and taking responsibility for knowledge more urgent, not less, since AI systems can generate confident content without checking whether it is true. He said the real question goes beyond whether students use AI for assignments, to who builds the technology, whose languages and experiences it reflects, who controls the infrastructure and who benefits, and called for humanities and social sciences to work alongside engineering and the natural sciences on its bias, power and labour implications.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, a cabinet minister setting out a concrete agenda, on teaching, assessment and research capacity rather than general debate, gives South African universities a clear mandate to act on.

South African Government News Agency (SAnews) · National government news agency

entry.title: UNESCO study finds 87% of Latin American and Caribbean universities already use AI, but only 26% have a formal strategy
entry.summary:
A UNESCO IESALC working paper with UNU-IAS, surveying 200 higher education institutions across 19 Latin American and Caribbean countries between August and October 2025, found that 87 per cent already use AI in at least one area, led by teaching and learning (74 per cent) and research (57 per cent), yet only 26 per cent have a formal AI strategy and 55 per cent have no dedicated AI budget at all. Adoption and governance both track institutional type closely: 84 per cent of private non-profit universities use AI against 68 per cent of public universities, and 17 per cent of public universities report no staff training at all, against 3 per cent of private non-profit ones.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the finding that AI use is already widespread while formal governance lags far behind, and unevenly across public and private institutions, mirrors the governance gap Wits AHEAD sees across the wider Global South.

UNESCO IESALC and UNU-IAS, reported by Times Higher Education · Established higher education press, reporting a UNESCO/UNU-IAS working paper

entry.title: UTeach survey finds STEM teacher-training staff cautiously optimistic about AI but wary of integrity and bias risks
entry.summary:
A survey of 57 faculty, administrators and staff from 31 university-based secondary STEM teacher-preparation programmes across 54 United States colleges and universities found 77 per cent agreeing that AI has the potential to positively affect their work and 61 per cent describing themselves as proactive adopters. Sixty-three per cent remained concerned about challenges, chiefly academic integrity (42 per cent) and ethical bias (21 per cent), and 70 per cent identified a need for further training; 79 per cent of instructors already address AI in their courses, mostly for lesson planning and assessment design rather than data-rich STEM inquiry.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, the gap between faculty already experimenting with AI and the shared, research-based framework they say they lack is exactly the kind of structured guidance teacher-training programmes across the Global South will also need.

The UTeach Institute, The University of Texas at Austin · University research institute report

entry.title: Systematic review finds no existing framework yet addresses the ethical and instructional challenges of AI in STEM teaching
entry.summary:
A systematic review by researchers at Wentworth Institute of Technology and the University of New Haven examined established frameworks such as TPACK, SAMR, ADDIE and Universal Design for Learning against AI literacy models and principles of responsible AI, for how well they support STEM instructors' teaching practice. It found that none of these frameworks has yet addressed the professional, ethical and instructional challenges of using AI in STEM education, and that adoption of AI tools is outpacing systematic pedagogical guidance, producing tool-driven rather than framework-driven practice.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, the finding that no current instructional framework covers AI's ethical and pedagogical challenges strengthens the case for the group's own work on responsible, STEM-specific AI integration.

American Society for Engineering Education (ASEE), North East Section Conference · Peer-reviewed conference paper

entry.title: More universities end Turnitin contracts as concerns mount
entry.summary:
Times Higher Education reports that Newcastle University and the University of Westminster have joined the University of Southampton in ending their contracts with the plagiarism-detection company Turnitin, after it proposed licence changes that could have let student coursework be used to train AI tools. Newcastle cited that data clause directly; Westminster said Turnitin's plagiarism checker was "largely ineffective" against AI-written text and its AI detector carried "a recognised risk of false positives". Southampton alone paid Turnitin £87,621 in one year, out of a student body of over 17,000 undergraduates and 8,000 postgraduates.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the dispute shows universities starting to weigh data governance and the real reliability of AI-detection tools against cost, rather than treating a plagiarism-checking contract as a fixed necessity.

Times Higher Education · Established higher education press

entry.title: Prepare students for post-graduation AI judgement challenges
entry.summary:
University World News has argued that higher education's response to generative AI stops too soon, at graduation, when the real test of professional judgement comes afterwards. It cites a 2026 preregistered field experiment in the journal Organization Science, in which 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants completed realistic tasks with or without a generative AI assistant: on most tasks the AI group worked faster and to a higher standard, but on one task set just outside the tool's competence, only 70.6 per cent of AI-assisted consultants reached the correct answer, against 84.5 per cent of those working unaided, and graders who did not know the answer rated the wrong AI-assisted recommendations as just as persuasive as the right ones.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, the finding that confident but wrong AI-assisted work can read as convincingly as correct work points to professional judgement, not AI literacy alone, as the capability graduates most need before they enter the labour market.

University World News · Established higher education press, commentary citing a peer-reviewed field experiment

entry.title: UNESCO and Codemao's AI coding drive reaches more African classrooms
entry.summary:
UNESCO and the Chinese coding platform Codemao report continued progress on their joint Youth Coding Initiative, which is training teachers and students in artificial intelligence and coding across Africa and Asia. Its second phase, running to 2030, has already trained 200 teachers in the Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Namibia and Thailand, 45 per cent of them women, and donated 200 tablets to 20 junior secondary schools in Kenya.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, this shows one model for building AI and coding capacity among teachers across the Global South at scale, with a deliberate focus on reaching women.

Xinhua (New China TV) · Major international news agency, video report

entry.title: PISA 2025 finds AI chatbot use split with student learning outcomes
entry.summary:
The OECD's PISA 2025 assessment, the first to examine artificial intelligence use among the 15-year-olds it tests, surveyed over 760,000 students in 91 countries. It found that heavier reliance on AI chatbots to draft schoolwork was linked to lower science scores, while moderate, guided use for learning showed different, more positive patterns; reading and mathematics scores also fell sharply across OECD countries over the past decade.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, this is an early signal of how the AI habits students bring from school will shape what universities need to teach and assess.

OECD (via Newsweek) · Intergovernmental body's flagship international assessment, reported by established press

entry.title: Understanding ethical dimensions of AI in higher education: insights from faculty members and students
entry.summary:
A mixed-methods study surveyed 971 students and 135 faculty members, then interviewed 23 students and 14 faculty, on the ethics of artificial intelligence in higher education. Both groups broadly supported using AI responsibly, but their views diverged: faculty stressed ethical principles yet reported a lack of institutional guidelines, while students found AI useful for learning but were unsure how far their own ethical responsibility went.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the study's recommendations, including faculty development, dedicated ethics courses and clear university guidelines, offer a practical checklist for institutions still without a formal AI ethics policy.

International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: From AI literacy to action: South Africa charts a path forward for teacher education
entry.summary:
South Africa's Department of Higher Education and Training and the Commonwealth of Learning convened a two-day National Workshop on Artificial Intelligence in Teacher Education at the University of Pretoria's Future Africa campus. Educators, policymakers and system leaders agreed on a flexible, principle-based national policy approach and set up a national task team, with the outcomes meant to feed into the ongoing review of the Minimum Requirements for Teacher Education Qualifications, which participants noted is currently silent on artificial intelligence.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, this shows a concrete, government-led process translating AI literacy into national qualification policy for South Africa's teacher education system.

Commonwealth of Learning · Intergovernmental organisation report on a national government workshop

entry.title: Supporting cost-effective AI adoption in education
entry.summary:
The World Bank has published a working paper, Costing AI Use in Education in Low- and Middle-Income Countries, with an accompanying blog post setting out how education ministries should budget for artificial intelligence. It recommends starting with teacher-facing tools such as lesson planning and feedback rather than systemwide student deployments, weighing AI spending against the existing cost of expanding conventional teaching, and building on devices and mobile networks already in schools. The World Bank estimates that reaching the Sustainable Development Goal on education in Sub-Saharan Africa would otherwise require an additional 6.4 billion US dollars a year for primary teachers and 38.7 billion US dollars a year for secondary teachers by 2030.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, this gives ministries and institutions in the Global South a concrete, costed framework for deciding where artificial intelligence spending in education will do the most good.

World Bank · Intergovernmental body blog, summarising a World Bank working paper

entry.title: Grappling with "homework scams", US universities shun AI detectors
entry.summary:
An AFP report carried by eNCA describes how Yale, Cornell and the University of Wisconsin-Madison are discouraging or barring staff from using AI detection software as evidence of cheating, after studies found the tools unreliable and prone to false positives, including against non-native English writers. A University of Wisconsin-Madison biology lecturer who hid a prompt in an assignment caught 60 of 350 students using AI undetected by conventional checks, and is moving toward oral exams and video debates instead of essays; a survey by the American Association of Colleges and Universities and Elon University found 95% of faculty fear students' overreliance on AI.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Generative AI in higher education, especially assessment and academic integrity, is Wits AHEAD's first pillar, and this retreat from AI detection software at leading universities is a direct, practical signal for how the group should advise on assessment redesign rather than detection as the answer to AI misuse.

AFP (via eNCA) · Established press (wire service report)

entry.title: Global Employment Trends for Youth 2026: Back to the Future
entry.summary:
The International Labour Organization's Global Employment Trends for Youth 2026 report finds that the global youth unemployment rate rose to 12.4% in 2025, leaving about 67 million 15 to 24 year olds without work, while roughly one in five young people, some 257 million, were not in employment, education or training. The report estimates that 6.1% of jobs held by 15 to 29 year olds are highly exposed to AI driven task replacement, concentrated in clerical and administrative roles that have already shrunk for young workers, and calls for a human centred approach to AI and technology governance alongside stronger support into decent work.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Graduate employability and just transitions, including how AI reshapes entry level work, is Wits AHEAD's fourth pillar, and this intergovernmental report's finding that clerical and administrative roles, often a first step for graduates, are most exposed to AI gives the group a concrete, global benchmark for its work on AI and graduate employability in the Global South.

International Labour Organization · Intergovernmental body report

entry.title: Generative AI use and misuse call for assessment reform in higher education
entry.summary:
A peer-reviewed study in the journal Science surveyed more than 95,000 students across 20 major public research universities in the United States during the 2023-24 academic year. It found that 37% of students used generative AI at least monthly for assignments, and the authors estimate that around 9% used it to cheat, with misuse climbing to 26% among daily users; cheating and use varied sharply by discipline. The authors call for assessment reform tailored to each discipline rather than blanket bans or university wide detection regimes.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Generative AI in higher education, especially assessment and academic integrity, is Wits AHEAD's first pillar, and this large scale study's finding that misuse varies by discipline rather than uniformly gives the group concrete evidence for designing discipline specific, rather than blanket, assessment reform.

Science · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: UCT summit puts AI, inequality and future of universities in spotlight
entry.summary:
The Times Higher Education World Academic Summit opened at the University of Cape Town on 30 September 2026, the first time it has been held in Africa. About 600 higher education leaders, academics and policymakers from more than 60 countries attended; Vice-Chancellor Mosa Moshabela said the future of the university could not be reduced to adopting a technology, while Higher Education Minister Buti Manamela called for AI to widen access to education, backed by broader AI literacy and better access to technology. UCT has already stopped relying on AI-detection software, building its own framework for how students and staff use generative AI instead.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Equitable access to generative AI in higher education is the first of Wits AHEAD's six pillars, and a minister naming AI literacy, not detection software, as the condition for fair access is exactly the ground the group's own policy and teaching work occupies.

TimesLIVE · Established press

entry.title: Global Index on Responsible AI: 2026 Report
entry.summary:
The Global Index on Responsible AI 2026, published by the Global Center on AI Governance and launched in Geneva in July 2026, assessed governance across 135 countries using more than 68,000 data points gathered between November 2023 and September 2025. It found that 126 of the 135 countries have at least one government policy or initiative on responsible AI, though this rarely becomes enforceable protection; AI literacy was among the stronger-performing indicators, with 71 countries, 53 per cent, reporting a framework in place, against far fewer countries with independent oversight bodies or monitoring systems.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy is Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, and this index's finding, that AI literacy policies are outpacing the institutions able to enforce them, names the governance gap the group's own policy work addresses for higher education in the Global South.

Global Center on AI Governance · Independent global governance research index

entry.title: Preparing future STEM educators: investigating artificial intelligence literacy among pre-service STEM teachers
entry.summary:
A peer-reviewed study in the journal STEM Education surveyed 541 pre-service STEM teachers in Lagos State, Nigeria, 345 women and 196 men, on their artificial intelligence literacy. The teachers reported relatively high AI literacy overall, and their knowledge and understanding of AI significantly predicted how they went on to use it; the study also found a statistically significant gender gap in AI literacy, favouring male students.

Why it matters for AHEAD: AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education is Wits AHEAD's third pillar, and a gender gap in AI literacy among trainee teachers in Lagos State is a direct signal for how teacher-training programmes across the Global South should design their own AI preparation.

STEM Education (AIMS Press) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Keeping the learning real: an integrated approach to academic integrity in the age of AI
entry.summary:
Wonkhe and the assessment service Studiosity reviewed United Kingdom university policies and held roundtables with institutional leaders and students in September 2026 on academic integrity in the age of generative AI. The report, published on 4 October 2026, finds that institutions are moving away from policing AI use with detection tools and towards redesigned assessment, AI literacy and non-punitive ways of validating that learning has taken place. It notes that the academic integrity system still lacks coherence and is not yet trusted by students, who doubt that institutions will believe their own account of how they used AI.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, this is a detailed, current account of how a major higher education system is redesigning assessment rather than simply trying to detect AI use, and offers a practical framework for guidance to staff and students.

Wonkhe / Studiosity · UK higher education policy platform report, based on institutional policy review and sector roundtables

entry.title: Digital solidification: learning analytics, the panopticon, and data coloniality in South African higher education
entry.summary:
Singh, of the University of Johannesburg, argues that learning analytics can act as a digital panopticon that fixes temporary setbacks, such as load shedding or a shortage of mobile data, into lasting deficit labels for students, within a framework of data coloniality. The paper does not treat learning analytics as inherently harmful but warns that flags which are never challenged or updated compound South Africa's unequal material and linguistic conditions. It proposes a social-justice-oriented framework built on data amnesty, participatory algorithmic auditing and contextual interpretation of flags as prompts for support rather than penalties.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This is a directly South African, peer-reviewed critique of the predictive analytics tools central to Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and predictive analytics for student success, and gives the group's pillar on responsible AI, ethics and equity grounded safeguards to weigh before recommending early-warning systems.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Helpful or harmful? Generative AI dependence, self-reported critical thinking disposition, and self-perceived employability among business students
entry.summary:
Shojaei and colleagues surveyed 412 undergraduate business students across three universities in Oman on generative AI use, dependence, critical thinking disposition and self-perceived employability. Greater AI use was linked to higher self-perceived employability, but higher dependence on AI was associated with lower critical thinking and weakened the positive link between AI use and employability, to the point of losing significance at high dependence. The authors conclude that the benefits depend on reflective, verifying use of AI rather than on the volume of use, though the self-reported, cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This speaks to Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI, graduate capability and employability, showing that uncritical reliance on AI can undercut the very capabilities employers value, a caution relevant to employability programming across the Global South.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Assessment practices resistant to inappropriate AI use in Open Distance eLearning: insights from Zimbabwe Open University
entry.summary:
Magwa and Zongozzi, of the University of South Africa, interviewed lecturers, students and a quality assurance coordinator at Zimbabwe Open University's Masvingo campus about which assessment types resist inappropriate use of generative AI. They found that performance-based, reflective, oral and closely observed formative assessments were seen as hardest to complete dishonestly with AI, though these raise concerns about lecturer workload and class size. The authors caution that findings from one regional campus cannot be generalised across the institution or open and distance learning more broadly.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This gives a Global South, open and distance learning perspective on redesigning assessment against generative AI misuse for Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, directly relevant to open and distance programmes across the region.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Automated software scoring of senior school certificate examination mathematical items in economics using a contextual similarity model
entry.summary:
Olaoye, Owolabi and Olaoye tested automated software scoring of extended-response mathematical items in senior secondary Economics in south-west Nigeria, drawing a sample of 1,008 students from a population of almost 275,000 candidates. The software's scores agreed closely with those of twelve trained human raters, with a high average-measures intraclass correlation of 0.863. The authors note the trial covered only two items and that each rater marked just 84 scripts, so further validation is needed before wider use in examinations such as WAEC, NECO and NABTEB.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This is a concrete, STEM-linked assessment analytics application tested at national examination scale in West Africa, speaking to Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and analytics in STEM and large-scale education systems.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Six publishers agree to feed 20 million research papers to AI agents, in a pay-per-use deal
entry.summary:
Six scholarly publishers, including Sage, the BMJ Group and the Institute of Physics, have agreed to let the Swedish start-up Redpine feed more than 20 million peer-reviewed papers to AI agents in real time, Times Higher Education reported on 6 October 2026. The pay-per-use deal compensates publishers and authors each time an AI system draws on their work, covering journals in medicine, the life sciences and the physical sciences.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the deal is an early test of how scholarly publishing can keep AI grounded in verified research rather than guesswork, while working out who gets paid when a machine, not a reader, does the citing.

Times Higher Education · Established press (Times Higher Education)

entry.title: Mystery-shopper study finds university enquiry replies 'costing enrolments', as ChatGPT outperforms
entry.summary:
A mystery-shopper study of 33 UK and 30 Australian universities, conducted by the consultancy Edified and the recruitment firm UniQuest and reported by Times Higher Education on 1 October 2026, found that only 37 per cent of around 700 prospective-student enquiries received a reply that encouraged them to keep engaging. Fifteen per cent of enquiries went unanswered altogether, and ChatGPT's replies were rated quicker, more complete and more persuasive than the universities' own.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, the study is a sharp reminder that institutions gathering data on applicants must also act on it, since nearly two in three prospective students in the sample were left unconvinced by a human reply that a well-prompted AI could have bettered.

Times Higher Education · Established press (Times Higher Education), citing a study by Edified and UniQuest

entry.title: How computer-science students actually use large language models varies sharply by task, study finds
entry.summary:
A working paper posted to arXiv on 1 October 2026 analysed how 211 undergraduates used large language models across seven modules of a computer-science problem-solving course. Students used the tools most in algorithms and web-development tasks and least in software engineering, generally treating them as assistants to be checked rather than authorities to be trusted, verifying outputs by testing in structured tasks and by web search in open-ended ones.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, the finding that verification habits shift with the assignment, not just the student, is a concrete cue for how academic integrity and assessment design should adapt task by task.

arXiv · Working paper (arXiv preprint)

entry.title: Cross-border virtual teamwork lifts intercultural readiness in data-analytics and machine-learning courses, study finds
entry.summary:
A working paper posted to arXiv on 1 October 2026 by Sehrish Basir Nizamani and colleagues describes a structured virtual exchange that paired undergraduate computing students in the United States and Pakistan for a six-phase, asynchronous data-analytics and machine-learning project. Students reported consistently positive experiences, and the researchers found that cross-cultural communication, more than technical skill, drove their sense of readiness to work globally.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, the study offers a tested model for the cross-border, asynchronous teamwork that Global South computing students need to build both technical and intercultural capability without leaving home.

entry.title: Copenhagen university appoints an anthropologist, not a computer scientist, to lead its AI strategy
entry.summary:
The University of Copenhagen has appointed anthropologist Morten Axel Pedersen as its first deputy prorector for AI, choosing a scholar of how people actually behave over a computer scientist to lead a 110 million Danish kroner strategy covering an AI office, task force, laboratories and a custom generative AI assistant. Pedersen, who previously directed the university's Centre for Social Data Science, plans to review every course at the university within a year to decide how AI should be used in each, and describes his three-year post as a temporary scaffold that will be dismantled once disciplines have their own rules.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, Copenhagen's choice argues that how students and staff actually use AI in practice, not only what a policy says, is the right starting point for teaching and assessment reform; Wits AHEAD reads it as evidence that governance of AI in the classroom is as much a human question as a technical one.

entry.title: UK research network to redo grant review after AI triage rejected half of proposals
entry.summary:
CRANE, a UK cybersecurity research network hosted at the University of Oxford and supported by UK Research and Innovation, has agreed to redo its review of a funding call after an AI triage process rejected about half of the 179 proposals it received before any human reviewer saw them. The network said it had used closed, secure systems rather than public AI services and that no proposal data would be used to train a model, and it has suspended funding offers already issued while every screened-out application is reassessed by its panel.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the episode is a caution that automating the gate to research funding without disclosure and recourse can shut out legitimate work before a person ever reads it; Wits AHEAD points to the reassessment, not only the error, as the standard any institution using AI in high-stakes review should be held to.

entry.title: Tshwane University of Technology dialogue presses South Africa to move from AI strategy to implementation
entry.summary:
Tshwane University of Technology's Institute for the Future of Work hosted its fifth annual Future of Work Dialogue in Pretoria, bringing government, academics and industry together under the theme of advancing Africa's resilient future through AI-enabled innovation. Senior director Tseliso Mohlomi argued that South Africa must move from AI strategy and debate to implementation, naming cybersecurity, cloud computing, AI literacy and data engineering as immediate skills priorities. The dialogue renewed a proposal, unmet since the previous year's meeting, for a National AI Implementation Council to coordinate government, universities and industry toward measurable outcomes.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, the dialogue's insistence on implementation over further policy work speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's concern that strategy documents alone do not create jobs; a coordinating council of the kind proposed is the structure through which university training could be matched to named, fast-moving skills needs.

entry.title: Liberia advances a national education data system to inform real-time decisions
entry.summary:
Liberia's Ministry of Education has concluded a national stakeholder consultation on a new Education Management Information System policy, backed by the African Union through its Pan-African Institute for Education and Development. Deputy Minister Thomas Momo Parker said reliable, timely data was needed for planning, budgeting and decision-making, as the ministry resumes its Annual School Census and introduces statutory school record-keeping booklets. The consultation, held in Monrovia with the European Union, UNESCO, Plan International Liberia and UNICEF, identified gaps in data governance, infrastructure, technical capacity and financing.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 5, analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, Liberia's move shows that a national data backbone, not only algorithms, is the foundation any Global South system needs before predictive tools or dashboards can be trusted; Wits AHEAD tracks such groundwork as the precondition for the analytics it studies elsewhere.
